hints: Think of ammonia as a base accepting a proton from nitric acid to form two ions, then combine those ions as the salt.
walkthrough:
See the proton transfer**
Picture $\text{NH}_3$ with its lone pair picking up $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HNO}_3$. That gives $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ which join together as $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$. No water is formed here because ammonia is not a metal hydroxide or oxide, it is a simple proton acceptor.
Final answer: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$

hints: Recall that heating spreads molecular energies out, so the most probable energy moves to a higher value and fewer molecules have that exact energy.
Remember total area under the curve must stay constant for the same number of molecules, so think where the new curve must lie relative to the old one at the start, peak and tail.
walkthrough:
Picture what heating does**
At higher temperature the average energy rises. More molecules are moving fast, fewer sit at the old most probable energy. So your new peak must be lower and pushed to the right.

Keep the rules of the distribution**
Both curves start at the origin because no molecules have zero energy. The total number of molecules is unchanged, so area under both curves is the same. That forces the new curve to start below the old curve, cross it once on the way down, then stay above it in the high energy tail.
Final answer: New curve starts at origin, with lower peak shifted to the right of original peak. New curve crosses original once and remains above original at high energy, tending to energy axis.

hints: Focus on the area under each curve to the right of $E_a$, this area counts molecules able to react.
Link that larger reacting population to collision frequency, remembering only collisions with $E \ge E_a$ and correct orientation lead to reaction.
walkthrough:
Read the area beyond $E_a$**
$E_a$ is the minimum energy needed for reaction on collision. The area under the curve to the right of $E_a$ tells you how many molecules meet that requirement. Your hotter, flatter curve has a clearly larger area out there.

Turn more energetic molecules into faster rate**
Rate depends on successful collisions per second. With many more molecules able to overcome $E_a$, the frequency of successful collisions rises sharply, so ammonia is produced faster. Collision frequency itself increases only slightly, the big effect is the fraction that is successful.
Final answer: At higher $T$ a greater proportion of molecules have $E > E_a$. So there is a greater frequency of successful collisions per unit time and rate increases.

hints: Recall that a catalyst provides a different route with a lower energy barrier, so think where a new $E_a$ mark would sit relative to the original $E_a$.
Apply the same area beyond $E_a$ argument as for temperature, but now the curve stays fixed while the barrier moves.
walkthrough:
Show the lower barrier**
A catalyst does not heat the molecules, it lowers the hurdle. Draw a new $E_a$ line, clearly labelled $E_{a(catalyst)}$, to the left of the original $E_a$. The Boltzmann curve itself does not change.

Explain the rate gain**
With the barrier moved left, a much larger area of the same distribution now lies beyond it. That means many more molecules already possess enough energy to react, so successful collisions per unit time increase and the Haber process can run fast at the moderate $450^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: Mark catalysed $E_a$ ($E_{a(cat)}$) to the left of original $E_a$ on energy axis. A greater proportion of molecules now have $E > E_{a(cat)}$, so frequency of successful collisions increases and rate increases without higher temperature.

hints: Use the given $\Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to decide whether the forward formation of ammonia gives out or takes in heat.
Consider how adding heat by raising temperature shifts a reversible exothermic equilibrium, and distinguish rate from yield.
walkthrough:
Spot the sign of $\Delta H$**
$\Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for the forward direction means forming $\text{NH}_3$ releases heat. It is exothermic going right, endothermic going left.

Apply Le Chatelier to heating**
If you raise temperature you add heat. The system opposes this by favouring the direction that absorbs heat, the reverse decomposition of ammonia. So although molecules collide more successfully, the equilibrium position moves left and the percentage yield at equilibrium falls. That is why industry compromises at $450^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: Forward reaction $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$ is exothermic. Higher $T$ shifts equilibrium to the left, to the endothermic reverse direction, reducing equilibrium yield of ammonia.

hints: Start by balancing $\text{NH}_3 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{NO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ by atoms, N and H and O must all balance.
Assign oxidation numbers using rules: H is +1, O in $\text{O}_2$ is 0 and in compounds is -2, then find N in $\text{NH}_3$ and in $\text{NO}$.
Link a rise in oxidation number to oxidation (loss of electrons) and a fall to reduction (gain of electrons) to confirm redox.
walkthrough:
Balance the equation**
Write $\text{NH}_3 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{NO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Balance N and H first, then O. The whole number set that works is: $$4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check: $4$ N, $12$ H, $10$ O on each side.

Track nitrogen**
In $\text{NH}_3$, $3 \times (+1) + N = 0$ so N $= -3$. In $\text{NO}$, $N + (-2) = 0$ so N $= +2$. The oxidation number rises from $-3$ to $+2$, a loss of $5$ electrons, so ammonia is oxidised.

Track oxygen to prove redox**
In $\text{O}_2$, O $= 0$. In $\text{NO}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, O $= -2$. The oxidation number falls from $0$ to $-2$, a gain of electrons, so oxygen is reduced. Since one species is oxidised and another reduced in the same reaction, it is redox.

Final answer: $4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
N: $-3$ in $\text{NH}_3$ to $+2$ in $\text{NO}$, increase so oxidised.
O: $0$ in $\text{O}_2$ to $-2$ in $\text{NO}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, decrease so reduced. Both occur, so redox.

hints: Count outer electrons: N brings 5 and each H brings 1, minus 1 for the + charge, and recall three N-H bonds are normal shared pairs while the fourth uses the N lone pair.
Remember to show one dot and one cross in each N-H bonding pair, place N centrally with four H around it, and add the + charge outside brackets.
walkthrough:
Build the bonding picture**
Neutral $\text{NH}_3$ has three N-H shared pairs plus a lone pair on N. $\text{H}^+$ has no electrons. When $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$, that lone pair becomes the fourth N-H coordinate bond. So in the end N is joined to four H atoms by four single covalent bonds.

Draw it in code**
Put N in the centre, H above, below, left and right. For each N-H bond draw a dot from nitrogen paired with a cross from hydrogen. Show only outer shell electrons, so eight electrons in total around N. Enclose in square brackets with a + sign to show the ion charge.

Final answer: Central N surrounded by four H atoms, each N-H bond shown as one dot (N) shared with one cross (H). All outer electrons shown in four bonding pairs with + charge shown, e.g. $[\text{NH}_4]^+$

hints: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on N in $\text{NH}_4^+$, there are four bonds and no lone pairs left.
Recall the standard angle for four electron pairs arranged to minimise repulsion with no lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Count regions of electrons**
In $\text{NH}_4^+$ nitrogen has four bonding pairs and zero lone pairs. Four pairs push apart as far as possible in three dimensions.

Name the geometry**
Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs always gives a tetrahedral arrangement, just like methane. The $\text{H-N-H}$ angle is the perfect tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$.

Final answer: shape: tetrahedral
bond angle: $109.5^{\circ}$ (allow $109^{\circ}$ to $109.5^{\circ}$)

hints: Think what nitrate ions do for plant growth when washed into rivers, and what rapid surface growth is called.
Consider what happens when that extra plant or algal material dies and is broken down by bacteria in terms of dissolved oxygen.
Link low dissolved oxygen and blocked light to the survival of fish and other aquatic life.
walkthrough:
Start with extra fertiliser**
Nitrate is a plant nutrient. Washed into rivers it overfeeds water plants and algae, triggering an algal bloom on the surface. This is eutrophication.

Cut off light and oxygen supply**
The thick surface layer blocks sunlight from plants below, so they cannot photosynthesise and release oxygen. At the same time, when the bloom dies, aerobic bacteria decompose it and consume large amounts of dissolved oxygen from the water.

Finish with the ecological effect**
Dissolved oxygen falls so low that fish and other aquatic organisms suffocate and die, reducing biodiversity. That chain from nutrients to bloom to deoxygenation to death is the full explanation.

Final answer: Nitrates cause eutrophication, rapid growth of algae / algal bloom. Algae block light so submerged plants photosynthesise less and produce less oxygen. Bacteria decomposing dead algae use up dissolved oxygen, so fish / aquatic life die from lack of oxygen.
